## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/01.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">The NCLB Growth Model Pilot Program
Discussion
Henry Braun
Lynch School of Education
Boston College

AERA
New York City, NY
March 26, 2008</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/02.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">NCLB (2002)
• Goals
– Hold schools accountable
– Improve learning for all
• Politics
– Federal framework
– State flexibility
• Theory of action
– Disaggregated reporting + Targets/Sanctions
==&gt; Positive Change
• AYP
– Sequence of cross-sectional comparisons
– Major technical problems</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">NCLB (2008)
• Empirical evidence on consequential validity
• Enhanced state infrastructure
• Minor fixes
• Growth model pilot program
– Partial remedy for problems with status-based
measure
– Counter perceptions of unfairness
– Maintain fixation on 100% proficiency by 2014
– Modify resource allocation</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">THIS SESSION
• Accountability system
– Measures*
– Indicators
– Decision rules and consequences
• Technical evaluation
• Sensitivity analyses
• Value judgments
• Suggestions for improvement

CAUTION: There is no statistical “truth” to be found here.
Validity is a function of context and
utility.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/05.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Allen &amp; Dunn

• Work within (new) NCLB framework
• Applied 6 approved growth models to a data set
• Disaggregated augmented proficiency statistics by
“achieved proficiency” &amp; “on track to proficiency”
• Overall differences are modest – but greater when
attention focuses on “non-proficient”
• Questions
– What is the GMPP trying to accomplish?
– Which model characteristics really matter?
– [HB] Should counts of “on track” students be down-weighted?</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/06.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Weeks &amp; Karkee

• Work within (new) NCLB framework
• Applied three types of models to a data set
– Simple gain score model
– Two-state transition model
– Mixed effects model
• Observed modest increases in the number of
schools achieving AYP
• Used models’ output to probe structure of
achievement growth</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/07.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Briggs, Weeks &amp; Wiley

• Working just outside the framework
• Most growth models measure change along a vertical
scale
• How do properties of the vertical scale affect
measurement characteristics of growth stats?
• Compared 8 scaling procedures (2x2x2 design)
• Calibration approach and model type matter
– Substantial differences in vertical scales
– Meaningful impact on inferences about schools for AYP
• [HB] Why not investigate non-linear models for growth?</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/08.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Ho &amp; Magda
• Working further outside the framework
• How do choice of standard stringency and time horizon
impact growth-based inferences?
• Each choice superimposes a grid on the multivariate test
score distribution
• Values of AYP indicators are a function of the interplay
between that grid and the parameters of the distribution
• Problem of how to “appropriately” set cut-scores:
Substantively or procedurally ?
• Tradeoffs as stringency of proficiency standards is
increased</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/09.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Betebenner
• Working well outside the framework
• Presents an alternative to growth along a vertical scale by
modeling conditional growth patterns
• Normative descriptions of conditional growth can
– Be highly diagnostic
– Serve as the basis for projections to achieving proficiency
• Identify students who have a “reasonable chance” of
achieving proficiency
• Explains why adding a growth component usually does
not make much difference in number of schools achieving
AYP</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/10.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">CONCLUSIONS (1)

• An important and informative set of papers
• NCLB consequences matter -- so examining
sensitivity of inferences to various characteristics
of the accountability framework is (should be)
critical to evaluating NCLB rules
• We understand more about where we have
robustness and where we don’t
• Current framework is problematic and can lead to
“statistically unnatural acts”</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/11.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">CONCLUSIONS (2)

• What are the real goals of school accountability?
• Which accountability system with what
“parameter settings” is most likely to succeed?
• How do we evaluate an accountability system?
• What are some suggestions for designing the
next system (beyond NCLB II)?
• When will we learn to do a better job the first time
and not have to rely so much on “salvage
operations”?</div>
```
